If you bump into your former tormentors, treat them with the same indifference you’d show a stranger who cut in line at the grocery store. You don’t owe them anything—not your anger, not your disdain, and certainly not your validation.  At the end of the day, the best revenge is living well, and it sounds like you already are. If you decide to go, let it be for you, not for them. Let it be a celebration of your resilience, not a chance to rub their faces in your success. And if you decide not to go, that’s okay too. Your worth isn’t tied to their acknowledgment. You’ve already won by building a life you’re proud of, far removed from the shadows of your past.

Why would homeless people rather beg on the street than get a job at McDonald’s? Homelessness is a complex issue, and the reasons people choose to beg rather than seek employment at places like McDonald’s are multifaceted. For starters, the assumption that someone can simply walk into a fast-food restaurant and secure a job is often oversimplified. Many homeless individuals face barriers such as lack of permanent address, access to clean clothing, or proper identification. These are basic requirements for employment that many take for granted. McDonald’s, like any other employer, has standards, and without these essentials, the application process becomes a non-starter.    Then there’s the issue of mental health and addiction, which disproportionately affect the homeless population. It’s unrealistic to expect someone battling severe depression, PTSD, or substance dependency to maintain the consistency and reliability required for a job. Begging, while far from ideal, offers a level of flexibility that formal employment cannot. They can set their own hours, take breaks when needed, and aren’t subject to the pressures of conformity or productivity.    Moreover, the stigma surrounding homelessness creates a vicious cycle. Employers may be hesitant to hire someone who appears disheveled or struggles with basic hygiene—circumstances often beyond the individual’s control. This rejection further erodes self-esteem, making the prospect of job hunting even more daunting.    It’s also worth considering the financial aspect. Minimum wage jobs, especially in high-cost areas, hardly cover basic living expenses. For someone already homeless, the income from a McDonald’s job might not be enough to secure housing, let alone sustain it. Begging, while unpredictable, can sometimes yield more immediate cash flow, which, ironically, might feel more practical in the short term.    Lastly, there’s the psychological toll of societal judgment. Constantly being scrutinized, judged, or ignored while begging is emotionally taxing, but it’s a different kind of strain compared to navigating workplace dynamics. For many, begging feels like a lesser evil—a way to survive without the added stress of conforming to societal norms that often feel alienating or unattainable.    So, while the question seems straightforward, the reality is anything but. It’s not about laziness or a lack of initiative; it’s about systemic barriers, personal circumstances, and the harsh realities of survival. Until these underlying issues are addressed, the cycle will continue.

Have you ever sabotaged food because someone was stealing it? I’ll admit, I’ve never gone so far as to lace someone’s lunch with laxatives or something equally nefarious, but I’ve definitely been tempted. Back in my university days, I shared a fridge with three other roommates in a tiny, rundown apartment. One of them—let’s call him “Mark”—had a habit of helping himself to my groceries without asking. At first, I thought I was imagining it. Maybe I’d just forgotten how much milk I’d bought or how many eggs were left. But no, it became glaringly obvious when I’d open the fridge to find my carefully labeled containers of leftovers emptied or my freshly baked cookies missing.  I tried the polite approach first: a note on the fridge asking people to respect each other’s food. That lasted about two days before Mark was back at it. Next, I tried confrontation. I told him directly that it was unacceptable to take my food without permission. He shrugged it off with a laugh and said, “Relax, it’s just food. I’ll replace it.” Spoiler: he never did.   So, I got creative. I started cooking meals with exaggerated amounts of spices—habanero peppers, ghost pepper sauce, anything that would make the food inedible to anyone but me. I’d label the containers with warnings like, “EXTREMELY SPICY—DO NOT TOUCH.” Sure enough, Mark ignored the warnings and ended up chugging milk straight from the carton to soothe his burning tongue. He didn’t touch my food again after that.   I’ve also heard stories from friends who’ve gone further. One guy swapped the sugar in a coworker’s coffee with salt for weeks until the guy finally stopped stealing his coffee packets. Another friend left a decoy lunch in the office fridge filled with raw onions and mustard, knowing full well the office food thief would be the one to take it. While I don’t condone outright poisoning or anything dangerous, I can’t deny there’s a certain satisfaction in knowing these petty acts of sabotage often achieve their intended purpose: teaching the thief a lesson they won’t forget.   Of course, the mature thing to do would be to address the issue directly or involve a mediator. But let’s be honest, sometimes the allure of poetic justice is just too hard to resist. Plus, it makes for a great story later.

Who is an actor who you think looks better older than they did when they were younger? Jeff Goldblum. There, I said it. There is something almost criminal about how the man has aged like a fine wine, becoming more enigmatic and magnetic with each passing year. In his younger days, he was undeniably handsome, but in a way that felt almost too polished, almost too conventional. Think back to his roles in the '80s—The Fly, Jurassic Park, even Independence Day. He was the quintessential quirky, cerebral leading man, but his look was still tethered to that era’s aesthetic: a bit too clean-cut, a bit too boyish. Fast forward to now, and it’s as if he’s embraced the full extent of his eccentricity, both on-screen and off. The silver in his hair, the lines on his face, the way he carries himself with this effortless, almost mischievous confidence—it’s like he’s become the embodiment of his own persona. Watch him in The Grand Budapest Hotel or Thor: Ragnarok. He’s not just acting; he’s living in these roles, his age adding layers of gravitas and wit that simply weren’t there before. And let’s not forget his off-screen charm—the way he speaks, the way he dresses, the way he seems to exist in a constant state of bemused curiosity. It’s as if he’s figured out the secret to aging not just gracefully, but with a flair that feels uniquely his own. Jeff Goldblum didn’t just age; he evolved, and the world is better for it.

My girlfriend is mad at me for "not standing up for her.” She accidentally spilled her drink on a girl in the club. The other girl threw her drink on my girlfriend and her boyfriend shoved me. I grabbed my girlfriend and we left. What should I do? First off, let’s unpack this. Your girlfriend is upset because she feels you didn’t stand up for her in a confrontation. The situation escalated quickly—she spilled a drink, it was returned in kind, and there was a shove. You chose to de-escalate by leaving, which, in my opinion, was the smart move. But here’s the thing: in the heat of the moment, emotions often override logic, and your girlfriend might have wanted to see you “fight back” as a sign of loyalty or protection.   Now, the question isn’t whether you should’ve thrown a punch or exchanged words—physical altercations rarely solve anything and often make things worse. The real issue here is communication. Your girlfriend needs reassurance that you’ve got her back, even if that doesn’t involve physical confrontations. Sit her down and explain your reasoning. Tell her that removing yourselves from the situation was the safest and most responsible choice. Emphasize that you care about her safety and well-being more than “winning” a petty argument with strangers in a club.   It’s also worth reflecting on her expectations. Does she regularly expect you to “stand up for her” in aggressive ways? If so, this might be a deeper conversation about boundaries and how you both handle conflict. Relationships thrive on mutual respect and understanding, not on unnecessary displays of machismo.   And let’s not gloss over the fact that this whole situation started with spilled drinks—hardly worth a full-blown feud. If this kind of drama is a recurring theme in her life, it might be worth considering whether her reactions align with the kind of relationship you want. Healthy partnerships are built on trust, not on proving who’s more willing to throw down in a club.   Ultimately, apologize for how she feels, but stand firm in your decision to prioritize safety over ego. If she can’t see the logic in that, it might be time to reevaluate whether you’re on the same page when it comes to conflict resolution. Relationships are about teamwork, not about who’s better at posturing in a fight.

What advice changed your life financially? The best financial advice I ever received was, “Live below your means, but within your needs.” It’s a simple statement, but its profundity hit me like a freight train. Growing up in a household where money was often tight, I developed a habit of wanting to splurge the moment I had a bit of cash in hand. It was as if I was compensating for all the things I couldn’t have as a kid. But this advice forced me to confront that mindset. It wasn’t about depriving myself; it was about being intentional with my spending.    I remember a particularly rough month when I had just started my first job. I was tempted to upgrade my phone, convinced I “deserved” it after years of using a hand-me-down. But that advice echoed in my head, and instead, I put the extra money into a savings account. That small act of discipline snowballed into a habit of saving regularly. Over time, it allowed me to build an emergency fund, which later saved me when I unexpectedly lost my job.    Another piece of advice that complemented this was, “Invest in yourself before you invest in anything else.” At first, I didn’t fully grasp what it meant. But I soon realized that spending money on education, skills, and health wasn’t frivolous—it was essential. I enrolled in a course that eventually helped me pivot to a higher-paying role. It wasn’t a life-changing decision, but it was a significant step forward.    These lessons taught me that financial stability isn’t about how much you earn but how much you keep and grow. It’s about making choices that align with your long-term goals, even when they’re uncomfortable. Today, I’m far from wealthy, but I’m no longer stressed about money. And for someone who grew up in a household where every dollar was stretched thin, that’s a win worth celebrating.

What has an employee said that immediately caused you to fire them? It was during my brief stint managing a small tech startup. We were a tight-knit group, and morale was generally high despite the long hours and occasional chaos. One day, during a team meeting, a new hire—let’s call him Mark—decided to share his “brilliant” idea for improving our product. Now, I’ve always encouraged open dialogue and creative thinking, but what he said next crossed every line imaginable.    “Why don’t we just scrape data from our competitors’ platforms and use it to undercut them? I mean, it’s not like anyone’s going to catch us if we’re smart about it.”    The room fell silent. Jaws dropped. Even the coffee machine seemed to pause mid-brew. I looked at him, incredulous. “Mark,” I said, trying to keep my voice steady, “are you seriously suggesting we engage in illegal activity to get ahead?”    He shrugged, as if he’d just proposed something as innocent as switching to a new project management tool. “Well, yeah. Isn’t that how the game is played? All’s fair in love and business, right?”    At that moment, I knew there was no salvaging this. Not only was he advocating for blatant illegality, but he also seemed utterly oblivious to the ethical implications of his suggestion. It wasn’t just a red flag—it was a flashing neon sign screaming “WRONG.”    I took a deep breath, leaned forward, and said, “Mark, I’m going to have to ask you to leave. Effective immediately. We don’t operate like that here, and we never will.”    He looked stunned, as if he genuinely couldn’t comprehend why his idea wasn’t met with applause. “But… but I was just trying to help,” he stammered.    “No,” I replied, my tone firm. “You were trying to compromise everything this company stands for. Good luck in your future endeavors.”    As he gathered his things and left, I couldn’t help but shake my head. It was a stark reminder that not everyone shares the same moral compass, no matter how clearly you try to set the tone. I’ve since seen and heard plenty of questionable comments in the workplace, but nothing quite topped Mark’s brazen disregard for ethics—and the law.

What movies do you like but everybody hates, and why? Ah, the guilty pleasures of cinema—those films that we secretly adore but would never dare admit in polite company. For me, it’s *Battlefield Earth* (2000). Yes, the one with John Travolta and his questionable wig. I know, I know. It’s universally panned as one of the worst movies ever made, a catastrophe of cosmic proportions, and the cinematic equivalent of stepping on a Lego brick barefoot. But hear me out. There’s something oddly charming about its sheer audacity. It’s like watching a train wreck in slow motion—you can’t look away, not because it’s good, but because it’s so *bad* it’s almost impressive.    The plot is absurd, the acting over-the-top, and the dialogue feels like it was written by someone whose only exposure to human interaction was through poorly translated sci-fi novels. Yet, there’s a certain earnestness to it, as if everyone involved truly believed they were crafting the next *Star Wars*. Travolta’s enthusiasm, though hilariously misplaced, is infectious. And let’s not forget the cinematography—everything’s shot at a Dutch angle, as if the camera itself is recoiling in horror from the unfolding chaos. It’s a visual assault on the senses, but in a way that’s almost... artistic?    Then there’s *Gigli* (2003), the infamous Bennifer disaster. It’s been mocked, ridiculed, and consigned to the dustbin of pop culture history. But I find it oddly fascinating. It’s a mess, sure, but it’s a *deliberate* mess, as if the filmmakers were trying to create a parody of romantic comedies without realizing they were making one. The dialogue is so stilted and unnatural that it circles back into brilliance. Lines like “It’s turkey time. Gobble, gobble” have transcended mere badness to become iconic in their own right. It’s a film that dares to be terrible, and there’s a kind of bravery in that.    Lastly, *The Room* (2003)—though I hesitate to call it a “guilty pleasure,” as it’s practically a cultural phenomenon now. Tommy Wiseau’s magnum opus is a masterclass in unintentional comedy. From the inexplicable football-tossing scenes to the nonsensical plot twists, it’s a film that defies logic, coherence, and basic filmmaking principles. Yet, it’s impossible to watch without feeling a strange sense of admiration. Wiseau poured his heart, soul, and apparently his entire bank account into this project, and the result is a film so bad it’s beautiful.    So, there you have it—my cinematic dark triad. These movies are flawed, baffling, and often downright unwatchable, but they’re also unforgettable. Sometimes, it’s the imperfections that make art so compelling. After all, life isn’t perfect, and neither is cinema. And honestly, isn’t it more fun to root for the underdogs, even if they trip over their own shoelaces on the way to the finish line?

What disturbing rumor turned out to be true at your school? It wasn’t so much a rumor as it was an open secret that nobody wanted to address directly. For years, students whispered about Mr. Thompson, the history teacher with the unnerving habit of lingering too long during one-on-one conversations with female students. His classroom was always impeccably organized, his lessons meticulously planned, and his demeanor oddly cheerful—too cheerful, some said. But it wasn’t until senior year that the truth finally surfaced.  One afternoon, a group of girls from the volleyball team decided to confront him after practice. They’d noticed his behavior escalating—unwanted touches, inappropriate comments, and an insistence on keeping them behind after class for "extra help." They reported everything to the principal, who, shockingly, had already received similar complaints from previous years. It turned out that Mr. Thompson had been quietly shuffled between schools for over a decade, with each new administration hoping the problem would just "go away."  The school board finally launched an investigation, and the findings were appalling. Letters from former students, some dating back nearly 15 years, detailed consistent patterns of harassment. Parents were outraged. How could this have been allowed to continue for so long? The answer, as it often is, was a combination of bureaucratic apathy, fear of scandal, and a misguided attempt to protect the school’s reputation.  Mr. Thompson was eventually fired, but the damage was already done. The experience left a dark cloud over the school and a lingering distrust in the system. It also served as a harsh reminder that sometimes, the most disturbing rumors aren’t just rumors—they’re red flags we choose to ignore because acknowledging them would mean confronting uncomfortable truths. Even years later, I still wonder how many more victims there might have been, and how many people knew but stayed silent.

Which TV shows were popular when you were younger that would flop today? Why? Growing up in the late '90s and early 2000s, there were a handful of TV shows that held the collective attention of kids and teenagers in Trinidad and Tobago, but looking back now, it’s hard to imagine them gaining the same traction today. Take *“Ed, Edd n Eddy,”* for example. The show’s slapstick humor and absurd antics of three boys scamming their neighbors for jawbreakers was a staple of my childhood, but in today’s climate, I can’t see it resonating the same way. The humor, while timeless in its absurdity, would likely be deemed too simplistic or even problematic by modern standards. The show’s lack of diversity and its portrayal of gender roles would almost certainly be scrutinized, and let’s be honest—kids today have access to animated series with far more complex storytelling and character development.  Then there’s *“The Osbournes,”* the reality show that followed the chaotic lives of Ozzy Osbourne and his family. At the time, it was groundbreaking—it gave us an unfiltered look into the life of a rock legend and his family’s dysfunction. But today? The novelty of celebrity reality TV has worn thin, and the show’s lack of narrative structure would struggle to compete with the slick, highly produced reality content we now see on streaming platforms. Plus, the casual substance use and chaotic parenting would likely spark outrage in today’s more judgmental social media landscape.  Another show that comes to mind is *“Lizzie McGuire.”* While it was a relatable and heartwarming series for many teens, its formulaic plots and predictable “life lessons” would likely feel outdated now. Modern teen dramas like *“Euphoria”* or *“Sex Education”* tackle far grittier, more nuanced topics, and Lizzie’s wholesome misadventures might come across as naive or out of touch. Even the fashion—remember those midriff-baring tops and low-rise jeans?—would probably be laughed off by Gen Z.  Of course, nostalgia plays a huge role in how we remember these shows. They were products of their time, and while they might not hold up today, they still hold a special place in the hearts of those who grew up with them. It’s a reminder of how quickly cultural tastes and societal norms can shift, leaving behind once-beloved gems that now seem quaint or even cringe-worthy. But hey, that’s the beauty of time—it gives us perspective, even if it means admitting that some of our childhood favorites were, well, kinda flops in the making.

The Good, the Bad & the Ugly is an amazing movie but I never understood the scene involving Tuco and his monk brother. As much as it was an emotional scene, it did not advance the movie plot at all. Did Leone ever explain why he added the scene? The scene in question, where Tuco reunites with his monk brother, is indeed a puzzling one, especially in the context of a film so tightly woven around themes of greed, survival, and moral ambiguity. On the surface, it seems like an emotional detour, a moment of introspection that contrasts sharply with the rest of the film’s relentless pace. But perhaps that’s precisely the point. Sergio Leone wasn’t just a director; he was a master of filling silence with meaning, of turning seemingly irrelevant moments into subtle commentary on his characters and the world they inhabited.   Tuco, as a character, is a chaotic force of nature—a bandit, a survivor, and a man whose every action is driven by self-interest. His encounter with his brother, a man who has chosen a life of piety and poverty, serves as a stark reminder of the life Tuco could have lived but didn’t. It’s a moment of vulnerability, a crack in his otherwise impenetrable armor. While it doesn’t directly advance the plot, it deepens our understanding of Tuco, adding layers to his character that make his later actions—both good and bad—more complex and human.   Leone was known for his deliberate pacing and his ability to craft scenes that linger in the mind long after the credits roll. This scene, with its quiet tension and unresolved emotions, feels almost like a spiritual interlude, a pause in the chaos to reflect on the choices that define us. It’s not about moving the story forward; it’s about enriching the narrative tapestry, giving us a glimpse into the inner life of a character who might otherwise be dismissed as a mere outlaw.   In a film filled with grandiose moments—the iconic showdowns, the sweeping landscapes—the scene with Tuco and his brother stands out precisely because it’s so understated. It’s a reminder that even in a world of greed and violence, there are moments of humanity that can’t be ignored. Whether Leone ever explicitly explained the scene’s inclusion doesn’t matter as much as the fact that it’s there, inviting us to see Tuco not just as a villain or a rogue, but as a man grappling with the weight of his own choices. It’s these small, seemingly insignificant moments that elevate *The Good, the Bad & the Ugly* from a mere Western to a timeless exploration of the human condition.

What should I absolutely not do when visiting your country? Well, if you’re planning to visit Trinidad and Tobago, there’s one cardinal sin you must avoid: assuming we’re just another Caribbean island where life is one long beach party rum punch-fest. Yes, we have beautiful beaches, lush forests, and a vibrant Carnival culture, but reducing us to a sun-soaked stereotype is a quick way to rub locals the wrong way. We’re a nation with a complex history, a melting pot of cultures, and a people who take pride in our unique identity.    Another thing you absolutely should not do is disrespect our food. Trinidadian cuisine is a sacred affair, and if someone offers you a roti, doubles, or bake and shark, accept it graciously, even if you’re not sure what’s in it. Turning your nose up at our food is akin to insulting someone’s grandmother—it’s just not done. And for heaven’s sake, don’t call our curry “Indian curry.” Yes, it has roots in Indian cuisine, but it’s evolved into something distinctly Trini. Claiming otherwise is a recipe for side-eye at best and a full-blown lecture at worst.    Also, don’t be that tourist who complains about the pace of life here. We operate on “Trini time,” which means things may not always happen when you expect them to. If you’re impatient or visibly frustrated, it’s going to be painfully obvious that you’re not from here. Embrace the laid-back vibe—it’s part of the charm.    Lastly, don’t try to impersonate our accent or slang unless you’re absolutely certain you know what you’re doing. Misusing phrases like “waz de scene” or “limin” can come off as cringeworthy rather than endearing. We’re a friendly bunch, but we’ll definitely laugh at you behind your back if you butcher our dialect.    In short, come with an open mind, respect our culture, and don’t try to force what you think Trinidad and Tobago should be onto what it actually is. Do that, and you’ll have an unforgettable experience. Fail, and well… let’s just say you’ll learn the hard way.
